notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1444.tmp1444.opp-lat: Scanning errors corrected silently where evident (UHTU = ORTU; Caria. tharbe = Cariatharbe; Alius = Filius; Nor = Hor; Pharga = Phasga/Pisgah; at mulia = et multa). Joseph: 'vere sub doto' read as 'verum sub dolo'; 'Saratofane' is the text's form of Zaphenath-paneah; 'Bresith' is unidentified; 'ministri regis' is odd as transmitted. Aaron: 'annorum ex XIII' read as CXXIII (123). Joshua: 'cum Dei' appears to lack a noun, probably 'arca'. Elijah: 'qui interpretatur Dominus' looks truncated (cf. 'Dominus Deus'). The identification of the widow's son as Jonah, and 'terra Arabon', reflect the text's own traditions. 'Tredecim filiorum' presumably counts Dinah, so it is rendered 'thirteen children'.

12: 'ullam' read as 'ollam' (pot); 'Jezi' taken as Gehazi; 'ex Abdelam' taken as Abel-meholah. 13: 'Ragel' taken as Rogel. 14: 'in amo carceris' read as 'in atrio carceris'; 'Cecis' read as 'ficis' (figs); 'Fadassur' = Pashhur; 'Anathoisdes' taken as Anathoth; 'iusserunt' read as 'miserunt' (let down). 15: 'unus Buzi' read as 'filius Buzi'; 'notas' read as 'rotas' (wheels); 'bonum castrorum' read as 'sonum'. 16: 'Sarira' unidentified; 'auri' corrected by the edition to 'Maurim', rendered 'field of Maur'. 17: text broken at 'solusque omnium Hebræorum ... sepultus est regione'; the sense of 'Principem namque super principem sibi posuit' is unclear; 'arietem præstantem' is uncertain (perhaps the ram 'being trampled'). 19: 'Dominum prædicare' is uncertain; it may echo Joel 2:17 ('let the priests say, Spare, O Lord').

20: 'Alios thesbites' is evidently a corruption of 'Amos' (the line names him Amos later); 'Tishbite' properly belongs to Elijah and seems carried over in error. 'ruborum mora distringens' rendered as 'stripper of mulberries from brambles' (cf. Amos 7:14, sycamore figs). 21: text broken after 'astra perculit'; the clause about Edom is obscure. 23: 'sub Jurat.' read as 'sub Joram' (so the Pseudo-Epiphanian tradition), though Ahaz's son was Hezekiah. 'Polyandreum' kept as a name ('common burial ground'). 25: 'a Secunda' taken as the Second Quarter of Jerusalem (Zeph 1:10); 'Silae' as a place-name (Vulgate 'Pilae'). 26: 'sub Zorobabel sacerdote magno' appears to omit Joshua. 27: 'De norne ejus' (of his name) may be corrupt for 'de morte ejus' (of his death).

29: 'ACUIs' read as Ahias (Ahijah); the text then says 'Ozias' died, evidently an error for Ahias, translated as Ahijah. 30: 'Abdo' is presumably Iddo/Addo, the man of God of 1 Kings 13, whom the text pairs with Rehoboam (biblically Jeroboam). 28 (Malachi): 'ad randuui' is corrupt; rendered tentatively as '[plainly]'. 33: several corrupt passages restored ('animam suam incontaminatam custodivit, in corde suo semper Domini sui memor fuit. Cum deinde...'). 34: the dates read 'VIII Kalend. Dei.' and 'VIII K. Junii'; translated as October and July, the traditional feasts (24 Sept., 24 June), since the printed months are evidently corrupt. 'Emiza' taken as Emesa.

36: 'collina aurea' rendered 'golden hill'; possibly an error for 'columna aurea' ('golden column'). 'virgo fecta' read as 'perfecta'. 35: the text omits Heli's death before 'Sine liberis'; supplied in brackets. 39: the bracketed 'Forte, Occidentem' is the editor's suggestion; the Vatican lies west of Rome. 37: the sentence 'Hæc omnia affirmant quo ordine...' is syntactically loose; rendered as two clauses.

In 41 'in nativitate Petro primus' read for the garbled 'in nativitate 1 elro primus'. In 43 'iuravit' (he swore) is read as 'intravit' (he entered), which the context requires. 'Achaia marmarica' as James's burial place is the text's reading; it is obscure (usually Marmarica is placed near Egypt). The date for Thomas, 'xn Kalend. Jan.', is read as XII. The final 'Lancea coi,,,' is corrupt; probably 'confossus' or similar, rendered 'pierced'.

46: 'filius Joseph Cleophae' is odd (perhaps for 'Mariae Cleophae'); translated as printed. 'Crito' (50) and 'Albanum' (47) are unidentified or uncertain places. 47: 'potuissem (ne)' read as 'potuissem me'; 'creature' read as 'creatore'; 'lassus liber' is obscure. 48: 'montibus Portorum' read as 'Parthorum'. 'Posphoro' taken as Bosporus.

53: 'vitis nuptas dederunt' read as 'viris'; the object (daughters) is implied. 'cornu.' before 'discipulus' appears to be a stray scanning artefact and is omitted. 'non lædet' read as 'non piget/lædit'. 55: 'arto' read as 'arte'. 57: 'Trientium' is unidentified (Lystra is expected); 'ovia' read as 'avia'; 'cum magno ... littore' rendered literally, possibly corrupt. 59: 'a nullis millibus' read as 'a multis/innumeris millibus'. 'clarior tamen lide et signi, sæculo' read as 'fide et signis'.

nodes.text: APPENDIX XX.
THE BOOK ON THE BIRTH AND DEATH OF THE FATHERS, concerning which see the Isidoriana, chapter 61, no. 48.
On holy Abraham, who was the first way of believing.

1. ABRAHAM, son of Terah, son of Nahor, brother of Haran, the father of Lot, father of Ishmael, and grandfather of Jacob. Eleventh from Noah, twentieth from Adam, he believed God with [his] heart, [and] received the Trinity as guests. He speaks with God, [and] is blessed by Melchizedek after the victory. He was granted a son in the time of old age, whom he offered to God for love of God. Born in Chaldea, he lives as a stranger in Canaan; very rich, he pleased God. Full of days, failing at 175 years, he died, [and was] buried by his sons Ishmael and Isaac in the double cave which is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, near the city of Kiriath-arba, which is also called by another name Hebron.

2. ISAAC, son of Abraham, born in his parents' old age, that is, when his mother was ninety and his father a hundred, born in Gerar between Kadesh and Shur, named by God before he was born, circumcised on the eighth day, obedient to his father, sacrificed to God as a figure of Jesus Christ, who was offered to God the Father. The wife of Isaac [was] Rebecca, daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, brother of Abraham, mother of Jacob and Esau. Isaac, full of days and an old man of 180 years, dies a just man, [and is] buried by his sons.

3. JACOB, son of Isaac, brother of Esau, supplanter of his brother. Blessed by his father, the father unwilling. Blessed by God, God willing, and his mother likewise. Born in Beersheba, made the father of thirteen children, he saw a ladder in Bethel while sleeping, beholding angels on the ladder and God in a vision; he wrestled with God [and was] blessed by him. He changes his name; he called him Israel. Very rich, he goes into Egypt because of famine; there he dies full of days, at 147 years; embalmed with spices, he was carried from there by Joseph [and] buried in the double cave in the land of Canaan, where Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, and Leah too, lie buried.

4. JOSEPH, son of Jacob and Rachel, brother of Benjamin, in Mesopotamia of Syria hateful to his brothers, beloved of his father, a truthful dreamer, is sold into Egypt by his brothers as a figure of Christ, who was sold for a price of silver. Sent to prison without fault, but through the deceit and lie of Potiphar's wife. The Lord was with Joseph in prison. He disclosed the dreams of King Pharaoh, which no one could interpret; for this he was honoured by the king, made prince of Egypt, and named by Pharaoh Saratofane, which in Egyptian means Saviour of the world. Nourisher of his brothers, and of his father as well, in the time of dire and heavy famine. He lived long, many days, 120 years. He died in Egypt, embalmed with spices, laid in the place Bresith in Egypt; Moses carried his bones with him out of Egypt in a cart, as he himself had asked, and in the time of Joshua, the king's minister, the people buried his bones in Shechem.

5. JOB, also [called] Jobab, whose father [was] Zerah, and mother Bozrah. Now Zerah [was] son of Reuel, son of Esau, son of Isaac; fifth from Abraham, a renowned king in the land of Edom. A simple and upright man, servant of the Lord. Rich and illustrious in sons and daughters, in possessions, seven thousand sheep, fifty yoke of oxen, and a large household. Proved by God, tempted by Satan, deprived of his substance, struck with leprosy, bereaved of his sons, much cursed, falsely consoled by false friends, and grieved in heart by their words, he speaks with the Lord; questioned by him, he reproaches himself. He did penance in embers and ashes; freed from the affliction, his substance is increased. Blessed by the Lord, he received double in life, and sons by the kindness of God. He lived after the affliction many days, 120 years; he dies old and full of days.

6. MOSES, son of Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob. Seventh from Abraham, brother of Aaron and Miriam, whose mother [was] Jochebed, daughter of Levi, son of Jacob. Moses, born in Egypt, hidden for three months, then put in a basket of rushes and let go on the bank of the river, was found there by Pharaoh's daughter, and named Moses by her; she ordered him to be nursed, and adopted him as a son. When he became a man, he visited his brothers. Having killed an Egyptian, he fled to Midian, and there was a shepherd of sheep. There he saw the Lord in the burning bush; the Lord called him from the bush and appointed him prince of his people. The Lord did many mighty works through him in Egypt, in the sea and in the desert; he saw the Lord face to face; [the Lord] gave him the law on Sinai, which the Lord himself wrote with his finger, from which he always taught the people. He saw the promised land, but did not enter it. At God's command he climbed the summit of Pisgah, and dying there he goes to his fathers, full of days, at 120 years. His eyes were not dimmed, nor his teeth changed; no one saw or knew his tomb, because the Lord himself buried him, and the people mourned him for 30 days.

7. AARON, son of Amram, brother of Moses, earlier in birth by three years, lesser in honour in many signs. Priest of God, prophet of his brother, anointed with holy oil, clothed in a splendid garment, he entered the holy place once a year, praying for himself and for the people; born in Egypt, worn out in the desert, he sins in the calf. His brother praying for him, he afterwards pleased God; he was deprived of a share of inheritance in the promised land, because he did not believe the word of truth, when the rock was struck in Kadesh-barnea at the water of contradiction. Angered at such a fault, the Lord said to Moses: Take Aaron and his son, and lead them onto Mount Hor, and when you have stripped the father of his garment, you shall clothe Eleazar his son with them by your hand. Moses did so, as the Lord commanded: he stripped the father, he clothed the son. Aaron dies on Mount Hor before all the people, in the fortieth year of the people's going out of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, when he was 123 years old, and there he is buried, and is mourned by the people for 30 days; and Eleazar is set up as priest in his place. His sister Miriam falls dead in Kadesh, and lies there buried by the people.

8. JOSHUA, son of Nun, who was first called Hoshea by his parents, of the tribe of Ephraim, servant of the Lord and minister of Moses, born in Egypt, strengthened in the Lord, and after his master's death made chief prince of the people. He sends spies into the city of Jericho; he speaks with the Lord, and heard from the Lord: I will exalt you today before my people. He crosses the streams of the Jordan dry-shod with [the ark] of God; in the plain of Gilgal he overthrows cities, tyrants, and kings of the nations. He commands the sun and the moon; the laws of nature stood still in heaven and earth. He sets cities and men together in order, and arranges them in divided lots. He always preached the Lord's law to the people, [and] judged Israel always in the seat of peace. He lived long, full of days, a hundred and ten years. Buried in Timnath-serah, part of his own possession, on Mount Ephraim.

9. SAMUEL, which is interpreted 'placed by God'. Son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, born of Mount Ephraim, born in Ramah, prince and prophet, a Nazirite from infancy, servant of God and minister of the priest Eli; his mother, who was barren, called Hannah, prayed to the Lord in the temple, and became fruitful. She sang the song: My heart has exulted in the Lord. Samuel lived faithful. He set Saul and David on the seats of the kingdom; he asked for rain, and it rained from heaven; he always prayed to the Lord for his people; he ruled the people many days. Very aged and old, he went to his fathers. The people of Israel mourned him, and laid him in the earth in his house at Ramah.

10. DAVID, son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, sprung from the tribe of Judah, born in Ephrathah, outstanding in beauty, king and prophet; he overcame kings, sang psalms, laid low beasts, killed Goliath, always feared the Lord, reigned mightily, foretold the birth and baptism of Christ. He showed forth his passion and resurrection; he prophesied the Ascension and his coming at the end to judge the world; chosen of God, whom God loved, humble and gentle, he fed his father's sheep; he reigned 40 years in Israel, 7 years in Hebron, 33 years in Jerusalem. He lived long. He slept with his fathers in the city of David, and was buried in Bethlehem.

11. ELIJAH the Tishbite, which is interpreted 'Lord', great prophet of God, still alive, servant of the Lord, a preacher to come, who will fight with the Antichrist at the end of the world; he fasted 40 days. He raised Jonah from the dead; he withheld rain for 6 months and three years; he made fire come from heaven upon whom he wished, and water. It consumed the ox and the stones and the water. Devouring flame killed a hundred and two men. This same Elijah lived in a cave, ravens serving him; he blessed the widow's oil and flour. He killed all the priests of Baal. He ascended up to heaven in a fiery chariot. He was born of the land of Arabon and of the tribe of Aaron.

12. ELISHA, which is interpreted 'salvation of my Lord', prophet of the Most High, disciple of Elijah and master of Gehazi, received the grace of his master; he divided the streams of the Jordan, and went through the river dry-shod; he turned bitter waters into the nature of [sweet] water; he sweetened a pot seething like gall. He called an axe up from the depth of the river. He cleansed Naaman, prince of Syria, who was stricken with leprosy; he struck his greedy disciple with the plague of leprosy; he blessed a little oil for a widow. The oil, blessed in a few vessels, filled not a few; the widow paid her creditor the debt, and with the oil set her sons free, and on the rest she herself lived with her sons. Elisha living raised a dead man; Elisha dead brought a dead man to life. Elisha was born at Abel-meholah, of the land of Reuben; when his mother bore him, a golden calf cried out in Gilgal with a great bellowing, so that the people in Jerusalem heard the bellowing. Then a priest who was present, hearing of the wonder, said: 'Today is born a prophet of things to come, who will destroy the images of the idols of the city.' Elisha died in Samaria, and was buried there.

13. ISAIAH, son of Amoz, is interpreted 'the Lord's offspring', an outstanding prophet in Jerusalem and a righteous martyr, noble in family, nobler in speech. He prophesied under four kings, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah. He beheld the Lord seated on a lofty throne. He heard the seraphim with twelve wings praising the Lord in a clear and solemn song, 'Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth'; one of them flew to him and cleansed his lips with heavenly fire. To the nations sitting in the darkness of death he announced salvation and light. He foretold a little child born of a Virgin, God and man, and prince, and father of the age to come; he prophesied a rod coming forth from the root of Jesse, flowering and bearing fruit with the sevenfold spirit; he foretold the overthrow and laying waste of Babylon. At the Lord's command he walked naked and barefoot for three years; he foretold that a chief corner stone would be laid in Zion. He announced the Saviour and ruler and most just judge reigning in Jerusalem; he declared the cross and passion, the tomb and resurrection of the Lord; he prophesied the judgement to come and that the dead would rise again. He preached in Jerusalem under King Manasseh; sawn into two parts, he perished; he was buried under the oak of Rogel beside the crossing of the waters which King Hezekiah had once blocked up with earth.

14. JEREMIAH, which is interpreted 'exalted of the Lord', prophet and priest, whom the Lord sanctified in his mother's womb; while still a boy, [born] of Benjamin, he prophesied; at the Lord's command he saw a watchful rod, and a boiling pot from the face of the north. He lamented the ruin of his city in a fourfold alphabet; he carried a loincloth at the Lord's command; he broke an earthenware jar in the sight of the Lord; the priest Pashhur put him in the stocks; the Lord showed him two baskets full of figs. He mixed the cup full of God's wrath for nations and kings; he carried a chain on his neck; he was shut in the court of the prison; freed from there, he wished to go to his homeland. Then the guard of the city held him again and handed him over to the princes, and the princes in anger had him flogged and sent him into prison again. But the king sent to him and drew him out of prison. The princes held him again, and wishing to kill him, they let him down with ropes into a very deep, dry pit. But the Lord, by the hands of Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, freed Jeremiah from the pit and from death, and he remained in the forecourt of the prison until the day the city was taken. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon freed Jeremiah from prison and from chains. So Jeremiah, born at the village of Anathoth, a little village three miles distant from Jerusalem, was led captive into Egypt and died at Tahpanhes, overwhelmed with stones by the people. He lies buried in the same place where King Pharaoh had lived, because, the serpents having been driven from that place at his entreaty, he made the Egyptians safe from the touch of asps; and the same Egyptians venerate him with great devotion.

15. EZEKIEL, son of Buzi, which is interpreted 'strength of God', prophet and priest of the Most High, led captive into Babylon with King Jehoiachin, in the thirtieth year of his age and the fifth of the captivity began to prophesy and speak to the captives. The heavens were opened to him, and he saw dark and wondrous visions of God. The word of the Lord came to him, the hand of the Lord came upon him in a great and wondrous vision, in wind and shining cloud, in fire and gleaming brightness, in shining amber; among these he beheld four living creatures with wings and feet and hands, a man and a lion, a calf and an eagle. He beheld four wheels beside the creatures, full of eyes on every side, and as the creatures ran to and fro together he heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of an army and of many waters; they bore on their heads as it were a firmament, and above the firmament as it were a throne set, and on the throne he saw as it were the face of a man, like amber gleaming in the midst of fire; seeing all this he fell on his face, and heard a voice speaking to him and raising him on his feet; it showed him a book which it held in its hand, and spread out the scroll and said to him: 'Open your mouth and eat this book'; and he ate it at once, and it tasted like honey, and filled his insides, and he preached to the people; he saw other visions of many forms, in which by the word of the Lord he foretold plagues to come on cities, kings, nations, islands, peoples; [he saw] a plain full of dry bones, upon which he saw sinews and flesh come, and as he prophesied the spirit of life entered all the bones; he saw a spiritual and wondrous city facing south, with gates, streets and many buildings, which could in no way stand in a bodily sense.

16. EZEKIEL is interpreted 'strength of God'; he was born in the land of Sarira, and was led captive into Chaldea, as we said before, and there the people of Israel ordered him killed, because they were rebuked by this prophet not to serve idols. So the people buried him in the field of Maur, in the tomb of Arphaxad.

17. DANIEL, son of Abda, is interpreted 'judgement of God'; sprung from the tribe of Judah, born in Upper Beth-horon, led captive into Babylon while still a boy, a pre-eminent prophet, with whom the Lord was. For he set him as prince over princes. For he revealed the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar: of the great image and of the great tree. He himself beheld great and wondrous visions: he saw the four great winds of heaven fighting on the sea, and four terrible beasts rising from the sea; he beheld thrones set, and the Ancient of Days sitting on a fiery throne, whom a thousand thousands of angels served, and ten hundred thousand stood by; he saw the judgement set and the books opened; he saw the Son of Man coming to the Ancient of Days; he beheld a great ram with four horns butting toward the regions, and a terrible and great he-goat fighting with the ram, and the ram prevailing; he set his face toward the Lord his God. In fasting, sackcloth and ashes he worshipped the Lord; with wondrous confession and pure entreaty he besought the Lord for himself and his people. For three weeks he mourned for the people; in his fast he ate no pleasant bread, nor meat, nor wine. Gabriel the archangel strengthened Daniel in all these things; he explained all the visions which he saw, and announced to him that Christ would be born and reign, suffer and rise again. He foretold that the kingdoms of the world would fight among themselves; he affirmed that the Antichrist would come and wage war with the saints. This Daniel showed King Belshazzar three terrible words written on the wall. He freed Susanna from a false charge. He condemned the wicked elders to death. He destroyed Bel, the idol of Babylon; he killed a terrible dragon with pitch and hair; he caused the seventy priests of Bel to perish. Habakkuk, carried in a moment by an angel from Judea into Chaldea, brought him a meal; the Lord twice freed him from the lions' den. He went to rest in Babylon preaching God almighty, and alone of all the Hebrews ... was buried in [that] region.

18. HOSEA, son of Beeri, is interpreted 'Saviour'; a prophet of the Lord, he preached the word of the Lord under five kings. He often names Ephraim, Samaria, Joseph, Jezreel, Israel, and the harlot wife and the daughters of harlotry, and the adulteress shut in her husband's chamber to sit a long time as a widow, and in mourning dress to await her husband's return to her. He preaches the word of God to the people, and rebukes their crimes harshly and terribly, and encourages all to flee and come to the Lord, because he heals, strikes and cures, and kills and makes alive, and loves mercy more than sacrifice, and seeks knowledge of God more than burnt offerings; and he prophesied that [God] would call Christ, the Son of God, out of Egypt. So this prophet Hosea, born of the tribe of Issachar, born in Belemoth, there slept a peaceful death and [was] buried.

19. JOEL, son of Pethuel, is interpreted 'the Lord beginning'. He describes the land of the twelve tribes as to be laid waste and consumed by the caterpillar, the cankerworm, the locust, the blight. He affirms that before the face of the Lord the earth trembles and the heavens are moved; he declares that the sun and moon and stars hide their brightness. He foretold that the great and very terrible day of the Lord is coming. He affirms that the Lord God is kind and merciful, patient and loving, and relenting over the wickedness of men. He calls the people to the assembly to sanctify a fast. He bids old men, young men, little children, nursing infants, bridegrooms, brides, priests, ministers of the Lord to proclaim the Lord, [and bids the Lord] to spare the people and grant peace; he promised that the Lord would give abundance of grain, wine and oil, and peace, to those who serve him. He foretold that the Lord would pour out his Holy Spirit on his servants and handmaids; he prophesied that the elders would dream dreams and the young men see visions in the Lord. The prophet Joel was born of the tribe of Reuben, born in the field of Beth-horon, and died in the same place, and rests buried.

20. Amos the Tishbite is interpreted 'powerful' or 'strong' or 'tearing away the people'; prophet, and shepherd, and countryman, and stripper of mulberries from brambles, he cannot be set out in a few words. For who will worthily express the three and four crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the sons of Ammon, and Moab, and in the seventh and eighth place Judah and Israel? He speaks to the fat cows which are on the mountain of Samaria; he testifies that the greater and the lesser house will fall. He sees the maker of the locust, and the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, or one of adamant, and an onyx boundary, and drawing out punishments for sinners, and a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God. He is the Amos whom King Amaziah had often beaten; but Uzziah, his son, pierced him through the temples and openly dealt the same prophet a deadly wound. So this seer, two days after he was carried into his own homeland, breathed his last, and was buried there.

21. The prophet Obadiah is interpreted 'servant of the Lord'; thundering against Edom, the ever-jealous rival of his brother Jacob, he struck the stars..... He rebukes the pride and haughtiness of the proud; he proclaims that the wise and prudent of the world, and its tyrants and strong men, will be struck down and perish by the Lord. He prophesies that from Mount Zion salvation and a Saviour will come, and the Lord will reign for ever. He was born in the field of Bethacaran and sprang from the land of Shechem, and was a disciple of the prophet Elijah, and the third captain of fifty, sent with fifty soldiers by Ahaziah to Elijah; Elijah spared him at his request, so that fire should not consume him as it had the two captains of fifty sent before him. So this Obadiah, leaving the service of Ahaziah, prophesied. He died and was buried with his fathers.

22. The prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, who is interpreted 'dove' or 'grieving', was the son of the widow of Zarephath, whom Elijah raised from the dead. The Lord sent him to preach in Nineveh. But he sought a ship and fled to Joppa. But God raises a great wind on the sea; the sea then heaves with great motion. The sailors toil with the wind and sea. They rouse Jonah, who was asleep, sleeping. They throw their vessels into the sea, they worship their god, they cast lots [to learn] by whose fault this danger was. The lot, once cast, at once fell on Jonah the Hebrew. Then they said, 'Where do you come from? What have you done? Of what people were you born?' Then he answered: 'I am the servant of the God of heaven, and a Hebrew by race.' Trembling with great fear, unable to keep silent, they said: 'What must we do with you, man?' The servant of God told them what they ought to do: 'Take me from this ship and throw [me] into the sea.' Then they threw him into the sea, as he had ordered. God sent a great fish to swallow the prophet; the fish swallowed him, as God commanded; for three days and nights the fish carried him, and from the belly of the fish he cried to the Lord, and the Lord heard him and at once freed him. The fish vomited him onto the land, which he had not wished; he went on to the city of Nineveh, he preached repentance to the king and the people. And when the king and the peoples heard, from the least to the greatest they believed in God, and in sackcloth and ashes not only men but also beasts repented; for three days and three nights they fasted, crying to the Lord, and God freed them from the blow which they feared. Jonah, most beautifully, by his shipwreck prefigured the passion of the Lord; he calls the world back to repentance, and under the name of Nineveh announces salvation to the gentiles. For those going to Tiberias there is a small village, where the tomb of this same prophet Jonah is also shown.

23. The prophet Micah is interpreted 'Who is this?' or 'humility'; sprung from the tribe of Ephraim, born in Morasthi, [the name] means 'heir'. To him the word of the Lord came in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. He calls all peoples to hear the Lord; he laments the ruin of Judah and Jerusalem; he rebukes unjust judges and impious men of power, and false prophets; he announces two robbers of the temple and of Jerusalem; he announces a lofty mountain prepared above all mountains and hills. He declares that all peoples and many nations will go up to that same mountain; he declares that the law of God, and the word of the Lord, will go forth from Zion and Jerusalem; he declares right judgement between peoples and peoples; he affirms that swords will be forged into ploughshares and spears into mattocks because of the greatness of the peace. He prophesies that a leader, born, will come forth from the city of David and will reign in Israel; he foretells that the cheek of the judge of Israel will be struck. He shows what is good for man, and announces what God requires of him: namely to do right judgement, and to walk carefully with his God, and to love mercy. He was not slow to foretell the persecution to come: that no one should trust his own wife, that sons persecute fathers and daughters mothers, that the daughter-in-law contends against the mother-in-law, and that a man's enemies are those of his household. He prophesied, as far as he could, the greatness and long-suffering, the mercy and loving-kindness of the Lord; he affirmed that the Lord casts the sins of the penitent into the depth of oblivion. This prophet, because he often rebuked Ahaz for sinning, was thrown from a very high precipice under Joram his son, and died. He was buried in his own land beside the Polyandrion, which is near Nain.

24. The prophet Habakkuk is interpreted 'embracing'; sprung from the tribe of Simeon, born in the field of Bethsachar. He prophesied that the Lord would come and be born from afar. He chastised the unbeliever; he affirmed that the just man lives by his faith; he terribly rebukes the greedy, the covetous, murderers, drunkards, worshippers of idols. This same Habakkuk, a strong and unbending wrestler, stands upon the rampart to contemplate Christ on the cross from afar, and to say: 'His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise. His brightness shall be as the light; horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden.' This prophet departed this life in the field of Sabarith two years before the return of the children of Israel from captivity.

25. The prophet Zephaniah, who is interpreted 'hiding her', son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, of the tribe of Simeon, prophesied in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah. He is the watchman and knower of the secrets of the Lord. He hears a cry from the Fish Gate, and a howling from the Second [Quarter], and destruction from the hills. He also proclaims howling to the inhabitants of Sila, for all the people of Canaan has fallen silent; all who were wrapped in silver have perished. He it is who prophesied that the day of the Lord would come wondrously and terribly, saying: 'Near is the great day of the Lord, near, and very swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be afflicted there. A day of wrath is that day, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast against the fortified cities and against the lofty corners; and I will afflict men, and they will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord.' This same Zephaniah died in the little field of Sabare (another reading: Sarabath), and lies buried in the earth.

26. The prophet Haggai, who is interpreted 'festival', prophesied in the second year of King Darius the return of the people from the captivity of Babylon, and the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel [and] the high priest. He promised, in the word of God, that God would give all good things to his people. He strengthened the prince, the people and the high priest, with the great help of God, to restore and build the temple of God, saying: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways; go up to the mountain to carry wood, and build the house, and it will be acceptable to me, and I will be glorified, says the Lord.' He prophesied that barrenness of heaven and earth, and of trees, would come for the sins of men. He prophesied abundance of grain, and wine, and oil, and abundance of peace and health for the people, and for the servants of God, and for those who serve him. He prophesied that God the Father and his Holy Spirit are always among his people, and [told them] not to fear, saying: 'Be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord of hosts, and act, for I am with you, says the Lord, and my Spirit will be in your midst; do not fear.' He prophesied that God himself would move heaven, and earth, and sea, and dry land, and nations, and the thrones of kingdoms, and that the Only-begotten of the Father would come, saying: 'Yet one little while, and I will shake heaven, and earth, and sea, and dry land, and I will move all nations and the thrones of kingdoms, and the one desired by all nations will come.' This Haggai came to Jerusalem from Babylon as a very young man. There he breathed his last, and lies buried in the ground beside the tombs of the priests.

27. The prophet Zechariah, who is interpreted 'mindful of the Lord', son of Berechiah — they prophesied in one and the same year, under one and the same king Darius. Zechariah in his prophecy is manifold and mystical. For, seeing various and obscure visions, he prophesied mystically, because the angel of the Lord spoke in him. For he saw by night [a man] mounted on a red horse, standing among the myrtles that were in the deep, and behind him red, dappled and white horses. He heard the angel asking about the time of mercy upon Jerusalem. He heard the Lord speaking to the angel good words, words of comfort concerning Jerusalem and Zion, [and] the cities of Judah. He saw four horns tossing Judah, and Israel, and Jerusalem. He saw a man holding a cord in his hand, and measuring Jerusalem in length and breadth, and saying: 'Jerusalem will be inhabited without a wall. For the Lord will be its wall of fire.' He saw an inscribed stone having seven eyes, and a golden lampstand bearing seven lamps, and seven pouring-vessels hanging from the lamps, and two olive trees standing beside the lampstand, one on the right and one on the left. He saw a flying scroll twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide. He saw a talent of lead which was being carried, and a woman sitting in the middle of a jar, who is wickedness, into whose mouth a lump of lead was cast. He also saw two women having wings, like the wings of a kite, who lifted the jar between heaven and earth. He also saw four chariots coming out from between two golden mountains: in the first chariot red horses, in the second chariot black horses, in the third chariot white horses, in the fourth chariot dappled, strong horses; and he saw many other obscure and mystical things. He prophesied the return of the people, and the restoration of Jerusalem and the temple; he prophesied that a poor and humble king would come, saying: 'Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king will come to you, just and a saviour, poor, mounted on a colt, the foal of an ass.' He prophesied that the same king would be betrayed and sold for silver, saying in his own person: 'They weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver', and the rest. He wondrously prophesied the passion of the same king, that is, of our Saviour, in every respect as it happened. For he says: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.' And again: 'What are these wounds in the midst of your hands? I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.' And again: 'They look upon me whom they pierced.' Of his name he foretold thus: 'And they will mourn him with a mourning as for an only son, and they will grieve over him as one grieves over an only son.' He foretold the baptism to come, saying: 'On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman.'

For of the death of this same prophet Zechariah I have a faithful witness, who neither deceives nor is deceived, that is, Jesus our Saviour in the Gospel according to Matthew, rebuking the unbelieving Jews and saying thus: 'May all the righteous blood come upon you that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.' Zechariah, then, having returned to his own land from the region of the Chaldeans as a very old man, and having been killed, as we have said, lies buried beside Haggai in Jerusalem.

28. The prophet MALACHI is interpreted 'Angel of the Lord'. He gives warning of mystical things and the mysteries of God, saying that honour must be shown to parents and masters: 'Let the son honour the father, and the servant his master.' In the person of God the Father he questions all the living, saying: 'If then I am Father, where is my honour? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?' He rebukes unworthy and guilty priests, who minister to God unworthily and guiltily. But he praises the worthy priest and calls him an angel, saying: 'Let the lips of the priests guard knowledge, and let them seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.' And he calls accursed the one who offers blemished gifts from his goods to his God, saying: 'Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock, and making a vow sacrificed a feeble one to the Lord.' He showed [plainly] that there is one Father of all and one God. For he says: 'Has not one God created us? Why then does each one despise his brother?' He foretold the coming of John, the forerunner of the Lord, saying: 'Behold, I send my angel before your face', and the rest. He prophesied the coming of the prophet and preacher Elijah to preach before the judgement, saying: 'Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, and he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the sons, and the hearts of the sons to their fathers.' And Malachi, at the end of all the prophets, prophesied openly of the rejection of Israel and the calling of the gentiles, saying: 'I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept a gift from your hand. From the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the gentiles, and in every place sacrifice is made, and a pure offering is offered to my name.' Malachi was born in Sopha after the return of the people of Israel from Babylon, and there he died as a very young man; he has a tomb among the Gibeonites, and lies buried in his own sepulchre.

29. AHIJAH the Shilonite, from the city of Eli, foretold to King Solomon that he would turn aside from the commandments of the Lord through women. So Ahijah died, and was buried beside the oak in Shiloh.

30. ABDO was born in Samaria; he admonished Rehoboam when he was sacrificing unlawfully. As he was returning home, a lion strangled him on the road. He was buried in Bethel in the tomb of the prophet who had deceived him.
31. AZARIAH is interpreted 'help of the Lord'. He was born in the land of Sabatha; and he died and was buried in his own little field.

31. ZECHARIAH is interpreted 'mindful of the Lord'; [he was] son of Jehoiada the priest. When he had lived thirty years, the people, gathered in the court of the house of the Lord at the command of King Joash, killed the holy prophet by throwing stones at him. The priests at once took him up from there and buried him beside his father.

33. TOBIAS, a holy prophet, servant of God most high, born of the tribe and city of Naphtali, was led captive to the city of Nineveh in the days of Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, among his fellow captives, young in age but old and wise in counsel and mind. All the good things he had he gave away in charity to his fellow captives. Though then a little boy in age, he was nevertheless perfect in the fear of God; he shunned vain idols and always kept the law of God. He ministered mercifully to proselytes and strangers. He gave worthy tithes to God. He took a wife named Anna from his own tribe, who bore a son, to whom his father gave his own name, and taught him the law of God and the fear of God. He always abstained from the food of the gentiles. He kept his soul undefiled, and was always mindful of his Lord in his heart. When afterwards he had favour in the sight of King Shalmaneser, he did what he wished and went where he desired. He endowed the poor of his race from the king's gifts. To Gabael, a poor man of his people, he gave ten talents of silver under a written bond. He fed the hungry, clothed the naked, buried the dead; [and] King Sennacherib, the enemy of God, wanted to kill him. But the Lord protected him with his wife and son. Afterwards he would leave his banquets, and hide the slain dead of his race, and bury them by night. In all these things he pleased God and displeased his neighbours, because he did all these things for God's sake. Then [God] tested him: he took away his property and riches, and struck him with beggary and poverty. He endured reproaches and mockery from his kinsfolk, and his wife, and his relatives. Like Job, he bore insults from kings and from false friends. But in all these things Tobias, the holy man, remained unmoved in the fear of God, always blessed God, and with groaning and tears begged the mercy of God; and the Lord heard him and freed him from all his tribulations. For he sent his holy angel Raphael from heaven, who strengthened him in all his counsels; [Tobias] thought him a man, and asked him to go on the journey with his son. So Raphael was the angel, as the holy father had requested. He set out on the journey with the son, and brought him safe to Rages, a city of the Medes. He talked with him as with a fellow servant and brother; he rescued him from the bite of the fish, and caused him to take as wife Sarah, daughter of Raguel, from whom Raphael restrained the demon named Asmodeus and bound him in the desert of Upper Egypt; and he gave great joy to the girl's parents, and received the holy father's money from Gabael, and brought Tobias back to his father safe and sound with great wealth, with his wife and a large household. He restored the light of his eyes to the holy old man; and he rejoiced to see his son and household. Then the angel showed them all the mysteries of his journey, and of Sarah's prayers, and of the healing; and the angel Raphael told them that he was an angel of God, and had been sent by God. Then they were afraid and fell prostrate on the ground, and the angel said to them: 'Do not fear; peace be with you; bless God, praise him, and tell all his wonders.' And when he had said this, he was taken from their sight; and for three hours they lay prostrate on the ground and blessed God, and rising, they told all his wonders. Then the old man opened his mouth and blessed God, and prophesied the restoration of Jerusalem and the temple, and foretold the overthrow of the great city of Nineveh. Very rich and illustrious, he lived many years with blessings. He was fifty-six years old when he lost the light of his eyes. For four years he was blind and poor. At sixty he received back the light of his eyes and double riches, and after he was given sight he lived forty-two years, and saw the sons of his grandsons. And so, having completed a hundred and twelve years, he departed in peace with the fear of God, and was buried with honour in the city of Nineveh, together with Anna his wife.

34. JOHN THE BAPTIST, who is interpreted 'grace of God', son of Zechariah the priest, of the tribe of Levi, born in Israel, conceived at an angel's announcement, named by an angel before he was begotten, born in his parents' old age, was made forerunner of the Saviour in a wondrous way: in being born, in preaching, in baptising, in dying, in descending to the underworld. For he was born six months before the Saviour, and beheaded before the Lord's passion, and descended to the underworld as the first herald of Christ: servant of the Lord, prophet of the Most High, voice of the Word, friend of the bridegroom, witness of the Lord, herald of the judge, lamp of the light, soldier of the king, end of the prophets, beginning of baptism. His father was silent, mute, for nine months, because he did not believe the prophetic angel; [John], when foretold, took away his father's voice, and when born loosed the office of his tongue; not yet born, he prophesied Christ and greeted him from the womb. Among those born of women none greater has arisen; the Lord praised him, named him an angel, and called him a prophet and more than a prophet, because he pointed out with his finger the one of whom he prophesied. He was full of the spirit and power of Elijah; when he appeared at his birth, he gave great joy to many. He recognised [the Saviour] in the dove, pointed him out in the desert, baptised the Saviour, preached repentance; his clothing was camel's hair, the wilderness his dwelling, his food wild honey together with locusts. When he forbade Herod to violate his brother's marriage, [Herod] ordered him to be consigned to the darkness of prison. The daughter of King Herod, dancing, asked for his head as a reward. And he, drunk among the cups, gave it, cut off, to the daughter who asked wickedly. He was conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, born on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and was buried in Sebaste, a town of Palestine, which was once called Samaria, and which King Herod, son of Antipater, called Augusta in the Greek tongue in honour of Caesar Augustus. But the head of John the Baptist was laid away with honour in a glass vessel at Emesa, by the gift of our Lord.

35. JOSEPH, which is interpreted 'increase', son of Jacob, son of Matthan, of the tribe of Judah and sprung from the family of David, born in his own city of Nazareth, a craftsman by trade, brother of Cleophas, husband of Mary in support, not in flesh. Cleophas was the father of the apostle Simon the Canaanite, while Joseph was the father of James, the brother of the Lord, who is likewise called James son of Alphaeus. Mary of Cleophas, that is, the wife of Cleophas, is the sister of the mother and virgin Mary. But concerning this same Joseph, husband of Mary, a rather obscure little question arises in the genealogies of the Gospels, that is, according to Matthew and Luke: for according to Matthew he is called the son of Jacob, in this way: 'Matthan begot Jacob, Jacob begot Joseph'; but according to Luke he is named the son of Heli, in these words: 'Joseph, who was [the son] of Heli, who was [the son] of Melchi.' But for those who understand the Scriptures well there is nothing contradictory in these words, for Matthew affirms him to be the son of Jacob according to the flesh, while Luke declares him the son of Heli according to the command of the law. For Jacob and Heli were uterine brothers, born of one mother named Estha, and not begotten by one father. For the father of Jacob, whom Estha bore to him, was Matthan, but the father of Heli was Melchi. When Matthan died, leaving one son named Jacob, Melchi took the same Estha, the mother of Jacob, who bore him a son named Heli. [When Heli died] without children, his brother Jacob took his wife, and raised up for his dead brother a son according to the command of the law, named Joseph, but according to nature his own son, that is, this Joseph who is called the husband of Mary and is declared to be as it were the father of Christ.

36. MARY, which is interpreted 'lady', or 'enlightener', or 'star of the sea', or 'star'; of illustrious lineage, daughter of King David, rod of Jesse, rose without thorn, kindly olive, golden hill, dawn of the sun, queen of women, bride of the Saviour, daughter of the living God, handmaid of the high prince, enclosed garden, sealed fountain, bridal chamber of the Trinity, mother of the almighty Lord, mother of the sun and of the flower, mother of the lamb and of the lion, mother of life and of the vine, mother of light and of peace, mother of the way and of the truth, mother of the servant and of the king, mother of God and of man, mother of the shepherd and of the bread, temple of God, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, holy virgin, perfect virgin, virgin before giving birth, virgin in giving birth, virgin after giving birth. The son whom she bore she believed to be the creator, and she had him as father, and worshipped him as Lord. She received the greeting from the angel, and recognised the mystery of the conception; she asked about the manner of the birth, and against the law of nature she did not refuse the faith of obedience. She was made the mother of a man without union with a husband; as mother she nursed the infant, and remained an uncorrupted virgin. Some assert that she ended her life by martyrdom. For thus holy Simeon, carrying Christ in his own arms, prophesied, saying: 'And a sword shall pass through your own soul.' Yet this was prophesied not of a sword of the flesh but of the spiritual sword, that is, the word of God, which is stronger and sharper than any sharpest sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit; for neither letters nor history teach that Mary departed from this life by the suffering of bodily martyrdom. This however is certain, that no one knows of her death, or how she departed from this light, although her tomb is certainly placed in Jerusalem. And so the Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of the Lord, is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of September, and her Assumption on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

37. JESUS CHRIST, which is interpreted 'anointed saviour'; for Jesus is a Hebrew name, which in Greek is called soter, and in Latin is called salvator. Christ, however, is Greek, which in Hebrew is called messiah, and in Latin is said unctus. This is the Son of David, son of Abraham, as holy Scripture [shows] in the holy words of the holy evangelist and apostle Matthew, who writes and says at the beginning of his Gospel: 'The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac', and the rest that follows up to the place where it says: 'When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of Herod, king of Judaea.' All these things affirm [his lineage]; in what order he was announced from heaven to the Virgin through the archangel Gabriel, and how he was conceived in the Virgin's womb, and in what place, at what time, under what king and among what people he was born, and how he was named by the angel, has been briefly told before. The greatness and height, the depth, breadth and obscurity of this mystery no one living by nature can, I do not say recount or search out, but even estimate, except he alone. But this mystery [is] as he willed, established and consecrated it, as the Holy Spirit affirms through Isaiah, saying: 'Who shall tell his generation?' And through the apostle Paul the same Holy Spirit cries out and says: 'O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God; how inscrutable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?' And again he says: 'From him, and through him, and in him are all things.' For who among angels or mortal men could search out, or think, or declare the true God and only-begotten of God, who is incomprehensible and beyond estimation, begotten before the ages without a mother, and true man, in flesh, soul and nature, conceived and born at the end of the ages of a true virgin mother without sin, without an earthly father? Or how can human frailty [comprehend] him? For he is God from himself and in himself, God most high, God in God, God with God, God in man, and man in God; true man in nature and humanity, true God in power and majesty. The Lord Jesus Christ commanded his Church to do what he himself did, to believe what he taught, to hope for what he promised. He deigned to come to us humbly, and to dwell among us in the flesh and in mercy for thirty-three years and six months. His conception and passion [were] at the spring equinox, and his nativity at the winter solstice; on the Kalends of January his circumcision, and his baptism in January; on the sixth day before the Kalends of April his resurrection; on the third day before the Nones of May his Ascension into heaven, where he reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever.
38. All APOSTLES are disciples, [but] not all disciples are apostles; for apostoli in Greek are called missi ('sent') in Latin. Disciples [are those] who learn fully.

39. SIMON PETER is called by three names: first by his parents Cephas, then Simon, third Peter. By these two names God named him: Simon, which is interpreted 'obedient'; Peter, 'recognising'. First a fisher of fish, afterwards he was made a fisher of men; Christ held him like a fish in the net of election when he called him to come after him. He is the one who recognised Christ, the key-bearer of the kingdom, the foundation of the Church, the prince of the apostles, son of John, brother of Andrew, sprung from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, which is beside the lake of Gennesaret. Third in order according to John, first according to Matthew; the first confessor of the Son of God, the beloved disciple of the Lord, and his denier. Praised for confessing, exalted for presuming, fallen by denying, purified by weeping, proved by confusion, crowned by suffering. His name is given from his deed, and a title is laid on him from the merit of his power. He shone in the world with miracles and signs; with the steps of his feet he trod the surging sea. His shadow passing by healed the sick; by his power he handed the living over to death, and by his might raised the dead to life. In mercy he restored their steps to the lame. He restored the slack limbs of paralytics to their proper state. He dashed to the ground Simon Magus, the sorcerer, as he was ascending to heaven. Under Claudius Caesar he founded the Church of Antioch, and under Nero he ruled the Roman [Church]. He preached in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia and the other neighbouring provinces. He is found to have gone about preaching to the Jews only; at the last, because of Simon Magus, though by the hidden will of God, he came to Rome, and there, preaching the Gospel, he held the pontificate of that city for twenty-five years. In the thirty-sixth year after the Lord's passion, under Nero Caesar, he was hung on a cross, as he wished. His feast day is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of July; he was buried on the Vatican, at the third milestone east [perhaps: west] of the city of Rome.

40. PAUL the apostle, who was first named Saul; Paul, which is interpreted 'wonderful' or 'pious', while Saul is interpreted 'impious'. Thus Saul, that is, the impious one, persecuting Christians; but Paul, that is, the pious one, preaching Christ to the peoples. A preaching shepherd, an illustrious preacher, the excellent teacher of the gentiles, the advocate of the Jews. Chosen by Christ, called from heaven, happily rebuked, thrown to the ground: he fell seeing, he rose blinded; a savage persecutor, filled with brightness, a vessel of election, a sheep out of a wolf. Last in calling, first in preaching; in the law a disciple of Gamaliel, in the gospel a servant of Christ. Born in Judaea, sprung from the tribe of Benjamin, labouring more than all, preaching far more widely than the rest, teaching the Gospel of God round about from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum; his miracles shine bright. Caught up, he ascended to the third heaven. By command he condemned the spirit of the python. He raised a dead youth. He struck the sorcerer with blindness; he restored to the lame man his proper gait. He did not feel the bite of the dread serpent, but gave it to the fire to burn. By prayer he healed the father of Publius of fevers; he endured incredible sufferings for Christ. From Jews and gentiles he bore blows, misery and toil, thirst and hunger, cold and nakedness; three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day sunk in the depth of the sea, struck by a thousand dangers and blows, thrust into prisons, bound with chains, handed over by the Jews to the gentiles. Let down in a basket over the wall, he escaped. Hemmed in by punishments, he suffered the fury of beasts; bound in prison, he was set free when an earthquake happened. He was baptised by Ananias in Damascus in the second year after the Lord's passion, and after all this he was in custody at Rome for two years; then for eighteen years he spent [his time] fully teaching the western nations, and under Nero, on the same day on which Peter was crucified, he was beheaded on the Ostian Way, and there buried with honour.

41. ANDREW, apostle of the Lord, brother of Simon Peter, first in birth before Peter, third in the order of the pontificate. By race a Galilean, born in the city of Bethsaida, he was first a fisherman, and afterwards became a disciple of Christ. While he was drawing fish from the sea with net and boat, he himself, like a fish, caught in a net, clung to the great Fisherman. Leaving net and boat together, he happily followed the Redeemer of the world. He followed the Lord Saviour, and became a fisher and preacher of men; he followed Christ even to the lifting up of the cross, and he manfully kept to his footsteps even to the suffering of the cross. For Andrew is interpreted 'manly' or 'comely': truly manly, and he acted manfully, for he preached Christ crucified to barbarian peoples, and wonderfully praised his cross, and wonderfully believed and prayed. So he preached the Gospel by the Caspian Sea, [in] Scythia, Macedonia and Achaia, in which he won many peoples for Christ. He was filled with the ardour of the highest love for Christ and for the cross of Christ, and in justice, holiness and piety he surpassed almost all. For when he saw the cross prepared for him, filled with unspeakable and inestimable joy and exultation, he said: 'O good cross, O glorious, O precious, O holy cross, adorned with the blood of Christ as with pearls, O cross so long sought and desired, receive me, I pray, and give me back to my master Christ.' He did not fear the cross, the minister of death, but loved it with exceeding love and embraced it. For he beheld his Master with incomprehensible love; therefore he did not fear the gibbet, though he felt it. Then he eagerly mounted the cross, because he obeyed his Master even to death. The blessed man, hanging two days on the gibbet and shining brightly with an angelic face, did not cease preaching to the peoples; the people saw and heard these things with wonder, and wished with great effort to release him from the cross, but no man born could touch him, because the Lord wished to lead his soldier to himself. Then he greeted the peoples and his brothers in Christ, and went joyfully with his Master and the angels into the rest of the kingdom. These things were done under the proconsul Aegeas in the city of Patras, on the day before the Kalends of December. The blessed Maximilla brought his little body from there with honour and embalmed the holy body with spices; his relics, that is, his arm, were translated to Rome in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantine, and were honourably placed in the church of the holy apostle Peter, his brother.

42. JAMES, which is interpreted 'supplanter', son of Zebedee, brother of the apostle John, first a fisherman by trade, afterwards became a follower of Christ; leaving net and boat, he followed the Saviour, leaving his father Zebedee. He obeyed almighty God. Leaving the sea and the fish, he became a heavenly fisher in the sea, that is, in the world. [He was] a preacher to the Spaniards and the western regions, and under Herod he fell, struck by the sword, and was buried in Achaia Marmarica on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

43. JOHN, apostle and evangelist, which is interpreted 'grace of God', son of Zebedee, brother of James. Son of holy Mary by adoption, and brother of Christ in virginity. Chosen by the Lord and so loved that at the supper he reclined on the Lord's breast. This John stood at the cross of Christ, and to him alone the Saviour, hanging, then commended his mother Mary. For this John wished to take a wife at Cana of Galilee, when the Lord Jesus made water into wine. But the Lord Jesus drew him to the example of virginity, so that a virgin might help a virgin, and the mother might have a son of her own. For when the mother received the disciple of the Master, he too was in a way left as another son in place of Christ. John, disciple of the Lord; John, archbishop of Asia; John, full of the love of God; John, a river of oil in the mysteries of the Gospel; John, seen as the eagle among the four living creatures in the vision of Ezekiel. Preaching the Gospel of Christ in Asia, he was bound in chains by Domitian Caesar; there he beheld the Apocalypse, that is, the revelation, where he both spoke and wrote the mysteries of God. But when Domitian was killed by the senate, John was released from exile and happily withdrew to Ephesus. There, at the request of the bishops of Asia, he wrote a Gospel, in which he surpasses the others in discourse, as he exceeds the others in love; among his other powers was the greatness of his signs. He was truly a martyr in will. For he was put into a cask of boiling oil and came out of it unharmed. He drank a cup of poison, and it did him no harm. He raised two men who had died of poison; he changed wild leafy branches into gold, and shaped stones of the shore into gems, and restored the fragments of gems to their own nature. He also raised a widow at the bidding of the people, and restored the revived body of a certain young man to the state of life; and, what is greater to say, he showed forth to the world the generation of Christ. In the sixty-eighth year after the Saviour's passion, under the emperor Trajan, worn out by the long decrepitude of old age, when he felt the day of his passing to be at hand, he is said to have ordered a tomb to be dug for himself, and bidding farewell to the brothers, he prayed; when the prayer was done, seeing the tomb, he entered [it]. Hence it happens that some assert that he lives, and contend that he lies in the tomb not dead but sleeping, chiefly because there the earth gradually wells up from below and rises to the surface of the tomb, and bubbles up from beneath to above as if with the breath of one at rest. But this dispute and opinion was removed beyond doubt from Christian hearts by a man full of the Holy Spirit, Pope Leo, the apostolic, [teaching] that the apostle John lies in his tomb neither alive nor dead; for, discussing this same John and the resurrection of the saints, he says thus: 'Indeed perhaps very many of these same blessed martyrs also obtained bodily resurrection with the Lord, or in consequence; for so we read that at the first festival of the resurrection, when the Lord rose, many bodies of the saints were raised and lived, and entered the holy city. But perhaps someone will say: The tombs were closed, the monuments built: how could they come out of them? Not to mention that all things are possible to God, and that he can bring forth a spiritual body from the closed inner chambers of a tomb, to pass over all these things, we have the example of the apostle, whom the tomb, having received him, could enclose but could not keep; for it lost the body laid in it, which it had taken in. For he was taken away by the grace of resurrection from the doors of the tomb, so that the burial stood, but the buried one was not found. Finally, when priests sought the body in order to honour it, the entrance was opened, [but] the tomb could not give back the one it had received.' The feast of this John is kept at Ephesus on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. Others place his falling asleep on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the nativity of John the Baptist is celebrated.

44. THOMAS, which is interpreted 'abyss', and by another name Didymus, that is, 'like Christ', for in bodily face he was made most like the Saviour; hence Judas too, betraying his master, said to the Jews: 'Whomever I kiss, he is the one; hold him.' To him the Lord deigned after his resurrection to show the wounds of his passion, because when the apostles affirmed to him that Christ had risen, he would not believe, saying: 'Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.' When Jesus came again to his disciples, the doors being shut, Thomas was then found among them; then Jesus says to Thomas: 'Bring your finger here and put it into the places of the nails, and put your hand into my side, and do not lose your faith.' Then Thomas feared and believed, and acknowledged his Lord God, saying: 'My Lord and my God.' So [the Lord] did many wonders through this apostle in the regions of India, which it would be long to tell you now; but those who wish to know them can find them wonderfully [set out] in his Passion. Yet one of his miracles, lest I seem to have passed over everything, I will try to tell briefly. Thomas was once at a banquet of the king of India, where all had whatever they all wished to eat and drink; but he would not eat or drink, but raised the eyes of his heart and body to heaven; and the king's cupbearer saw this, came angrily to the apostle, struck him a slap in the face, and said: 'Why do you not eat and drink of the feast and the wine at the king's banquet?' Then Thomas, answering in Hebrew, said to him: 'I will not leave this banquet until a black dog lays down your right hand in the middle [of it].' No one at the banquet understood these words except one Hebrew girl, who was playing the cithara for the guests. It came about as the man of God said: the cupbearer went outside to fetch water; a lion met him on the way, which strangled him to death and broke all his bones to pieces. Dogs from the king's palace came together to the corpse [and] divided the accursed man's limbs among themselves. Of these one black dog brought the cupbearer's right hand into the middle of the banquet, as Thomas, the man of God, had foretold. When the Hebrew girl saw this, she came to the apostle playing the cithara, and stood before him sounding songs on the cithara, and, filled with faith and the ardour of the love of God, she began to sing a spiritual song with the cithara and wonderfully to praise the almighty God of all, saying: 'One God of the Hebrews, who created all things; he made heaven and earth, and founded the seas.' When at the apostle's command she had sung this again, she bowed at his feet with great faith, and devoutly believed in Christ the Saviour of all. All the peoples, when they saw and heard these things, marvelled greatly and were afraid, and many of them believed in Christ. So this Thomas preached to the Parthians and Medes and the innermost eastern region, and there he preached the Gospel and suffered martyrdom. Pierced there with a lance, he fell in Calamina, a city of India, and there he was buried with honour on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

45. PHILIP, which is interpreted 'mouth of a lamp', sprang from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter; his memory is read in the Acts of the Apostles. He was one of the seven deacons who were ordained by the apostles together with saint Stephen, and their names are these: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus and Nicanor, Timothy and Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch. This Philip had a wife, and he fathered four daughters by her who were prophetesses, and afterwards he was an apostle of the Lord. He went to Samaria filled with the power of the Lord; there he first preached the word of the Lord to the Samaritans, and in him there was such power of divine grace that by his preaching he confounded even Simon Magus, who at that same time was held in great renown among the peoples of Samaria, so that he was thought to be the great power of God. But when he had seen the signs and miracles that were done by Philip through the might of divine grace, he gave way, astounded and terrified, and pretended to believe in Christ, to the point that he even received baptism. Then Philip preached Christ to the Gauls, afterwards in Hierapolis of the province of Phrygia, where he died crucified and stoned, and there he rests with his daughters. His feast day is celebrated on the Kalends of May.

46. JAMES, which is interpreted 'supplanter', son of Joseph [and] of Cleophas, whose memory is read in the Gospel. This James is read [to be] the brother of the apostle Thaddaeus, which Thaddaeus is called by another name Judas, and both are called brothers of Christ. This same James was the first bishop of Jerusalem; he was surnamed the Just and bishop of the apostles. There were many Jameses, but this James of Alphaeus, who, as we said before, was surnamed the Just, surpasses the other Jameses, because he was always holy from his mother's womb: he did not drink wine or strong drink, and did not eat meat; iron never came upon his head, he was not anointed with oil, he was not washed whole in a bath, nor clothed in wool, but dressed only in a linen cloth. To him alone was it permitted to enter the Holy of Holies; he alone used to go into the temple, and he would lie so on his knees praying for the pardon of the people that by praying he made calluses on his knees like a camel's, always bending the knees and never ceasing from prayer. And so for this incredible continence and supreme justice he was called the Just, and Oblias, which is interpreted 'bulwark of the people'. While he was preaching in Jerusalem Christ the Son of God, he was thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple, and, struck on the head with a fuller's club, he was crushed with stones by the Jews, and there beside the temple he was buried. His feast day and ordination are believed [to fall] on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

47. The apostle BARTHOLOMEW, who took his name from the Syrian language, and it is interpreted 'son of the one who suspends the waters'. He was well made in form, handsome in face and eyes, [with] splendid clothing and gems, yet not elated by this, nor proud. To him the Lord gave such power over demons that, when he wished, the demons in the idols fell silent, and when he wished, the demons, against their will, displayed and proclaimed from the idols their foulness and miseries. It happened once that Bartholomew showed such a miracle among the people, when he ordered the people to stand before an idol, and in the power of God commanded the demon to come out of the idol and show itself to the people in its great misery and deformity, and to proclaim [it]. Then the wretch, unwilling, with groaning and howling, began to say: 'O fools, see what a god you have worshipped in unhappy me! O senseless ones, consider me, wretched and misshapen and despised in every way, whom you asked [to be your] helper. O misled ones, behold what a lord you have believed in with most foolish and blind heart. O deceived ones, attend, for I am not God, but a most wretched demon, deceived in pride and fallen from heaven; I was once an angel in glory, now I have become a devil in the wrath of God. I lost glory and the angelic life in heaven, and found endless and countless punishments in hell, and I have so lost my glory that in no way can I find pardon or the grace of the Lord, because I have no flesh, nor the matter for penance. For if I, wretch, could have had one finger with a nail of human flesh, I could have redeemed myself from my misery and cruelty. You senseless ones, created with all [things], and made after the two images of God, why do you mislead and destroy yourselves? Why do you stray from the Creator, when he himself gave you feet for standing and walking, hands for touching and working, eyes for seeing and knowing, ears for hearing, a tongue for speaking and praising God, a heart for believing and understanding?' Then the apostle answered him: 'How could you, wretch, have redeemed yourself from your calamity with one finger of a man with a nail?' He answered him again with a howl: 'With that one finger and nail I would have cleaned the nostrils of one, the ears of another, the eyes of a third, and I would have scratched the limbs of all as they wished, and I would have done these things diligently. One perhaps would have said: "God bless you"; another: "God help you"; a third: "God deliver you from evil"; and in these many great blessings, [though] weary, I would have come [out] free.' And when he had said all these things at God's command and against his own will, the wretch vanished from the eyes of all. Then all the people, when they saw and heard these things, were greatly afraid and amazed; and abandoning the vain [worship] of idols, they believed and blessed almighty God. So this Bartholomew preached to Lycaonia. At the last, in Albanum, a greater city of Armenia, he was flayed alive by barbarians, and beheaded by order of King Astyages, and so buried in the earth on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

48. The apostle and evangelist MATTHEW took his name from the city of Matthea, and it is interpreted 'given'; first a publican, afterwards a disciple of the Lord. He sat at the tax booth, managed treasures, sinned publicly, darkened within, blinded by care for the world. At length, God willing, he saw the sun of justice, he heard with the ear of the heart the words of truth; he followed the sun which he saw, the truth which he heard he believed and adored: leaving the tax booth, he followed the Lord of all; leaving perishable treasure, he followed the king who abides for ever; leaving falsehood and vanity, he followed the way and the truth; leaving death and the world, he followed life and the kingdom; forgetting foolish talk, he writes and preaches the Gospel. He was called by three names, that is, Matthew, Levi, Publican. Matthew, named from his city Matthea, as we said before; Levi from the tribe of Levi, from which he sprang; hence surnamed Publican, because he kept the public [revenues]. Matthew is interpreted 'given'; Levi 'minister'; publican, because he sins publicly. First he wrote the Gospel in Judaea in the time of Gaius, emperor of Rome, and preached, and afterwards in Macedonia; and having suffered in Persia on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, he rests in glory in the mountains of the Parthians.

49. SIMON ZELOTES, which is interpreted 'zeal'. He was first called the Canaanite from the village of Cana, which is interpreted 'possessing'; he was also called Simon by a third name, burning with zeal for God. [He was] Peter's equal in name, and like him in honour. Apostle of the Lord and [his] cousin, son of Cleophas and Mary, the Mary who is called [wife] of Cleophas in the Gospel. Cleophas his father and Joseph, who is called as it were the father of Christ, were brothers, and his mother, who is called Mary of Cleophas, was the sister of Mary the mother of the Lord. Thus in wonderful fashion two brothers had two sisters as wives, but Cleophas carnally, Joseph spiritually. So this Simon received the primacy in preaching in Egypt, and after James the Just he is said to have held the see of Jerusalem, and after 120 years he was found worthy under the emperor Hadrian to endure the martyrdom of suffering by the cross. He lies in the Bosporus; his feast is on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

50. JUDAS LEBBAEUS, that is, 'little heart', that is, from 'heart'; he is also Thaddaeus, he is Judas of James, son of Joseph the brother of Cleophas, and he is interpreted 'confessor'. He preached in Mesopotamia and the interior of Pontus. He was buried in Crito, a city of Armenia; his feast is celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

51. MATTHIAS, or MATTHIAN, was one of the seventy disciples, and was substituted among the apostles in place of Judas Iscariot. Chosen by lot, and alone without a surname, to him was given the preaching of the Gospel in Judaea.

52. These holy apostles were the disciples of Christ, lights of the world, precious stones, friends of the Saviour, preachers of the faith, groomsmen of the bridegroom, princes of the world, key-bearers of the kingdom, the salt of the earth, branches on the true vine, sowers of justice, reapers in the householder's crop, lovers of truth, teachers of the nations, conquerors of demons and tyrants, explorers of paradise, good shepherds of Christ's sheep, judges of the Jews at the great judgement, sitting with the Judge upon twelve thrones. Though they are all one, yet each of them received his own lot for preaching in particular and fixed places in the world: Peter Rome, Paul from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, Andrew Achaia, James of Zebedee Spain, John his brother Asia, Thomas India, James the brother of Jude Jerusalem, Matthew Macedonia, Philip the Gauls, Bartholomew Lycaonia, Simon Zelotes Egypt, Judas Mesopotamia, Matthias Judaea.

53. CONCERNING THE APOSTLES, who without doubt had wives, I have heard Saint Clement say as follows, who was their companion and disciple, and was the third pope in Rome after Peter; for he says this: Peter and Philip both had wives, and they also gave [their daughters] married to husbands; and indeed it does not trouble the apostle Paul, in one of his Epistles, to make mention of and greet his partner, whom he nevertheless declines to take around with him, so that he might be freer for the preaching of the Gospel. So too it is said of Peter. They say, he says, that blessed Peter, when he saw his wife being led to her passion, rejoiced at the grace of her election and of her return to her own home, and called out after her as she was led, and, addressing her by her own name, said: 'O wife, remember the Lord.' Such were the marriages of the saints, so perfect was the affection of the blessed.

54. MARK, who is interpreted 'exalted', evangelist of God and son of Peter in baptism, and his disciple in the divine word. He exercised the priesthood in Israel, being a Levite according to the flesh. Converted to the faith of Christ, he wrote the Gospel in Italy in the time of Claudius Caesar. After [coming to] the faith he is said to have cut off his thumb, so that he would be held unfit for the priesthood; but according to the dispensation of God and the merit of his faith, and of his life, he was afterwards made a bishop. For they relate that this Mark first went to Egypt, and there preached the Gospel which he himself had written; and this is called a praiseworthy theft, because what Peter had preached by word, he, asked by the brethren, wrote down in secret.
